line-of-aisling.description: Aisling and her line, as the copyists kept it.

line-of-the-mason.description: Neachdan the mason and his descendants, from the first fire to the end of the line.

the-library.description: The Library at Muileann chaol and the record it keeps.

the-mist.description: Manannan's mist, which hid the island from the ships beyond it, and its thinning.

the-orders-of-the-old-faith.gloss: the orders of the Old Faith
the-orders-of-the-old-faith.description: The orders of An Creideamh Sean, the Old Faith: their founding, rules and quarrels.

the-seven-coals.description: The seven coals of the vein: their finding, their lighting, their rule and their failing.

the-seven-houses.description: The custodian houses of the vein, their rolls and their lots, from the first houses made after the Sundering through the crown joined to the vein, to the council of the seven heads that sat in the empty chair's stead.

the-small-burning-law.gloss: the Law of the Small Burning
the-small-burning-law.description: The rule that the vein-coal be burned only in small measure and only by the custodians, first written in the custody-book at the vein-house and kept, argued and bent through the whole Age of Sundering.

the-stone-kings.description: The Stone Kings of the Age of Ailean and what was remembered of them.

the-sundering.description: The fleet that sailed into the mist and never came back, the island left alone in the world, and the long learning to live cut off: the numbering of the ships, the empty places laid, the watch on the headlands and its lapsing.

ailean-mac-dhughaill-scholar.name: Ailean mac Dhùghaill (scholar of Dùn thais)

ailean-mac-raghnaill-iv.name: Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth of the name

domhnall-mac-ailein-stone.name: Dòmhnall mac Ailein (preacher of the Stone)

donnchadh-mac-thormoid-clerk.name: Donnchadh mac Thormoid (clerk of the vein-house)

dughall-mac-iain-fisher.name: Dùghall mac Iain (fisher of Inis àrsaidh)

eilidh-nic-ruairidh-grove.name: Eilidh nic Ruairidh (grove-keeper of Doire fhionn)

events.title: Land is found
events.body: Word comes of a land across the open water, where no people like the Dia-thìrich dwell. Who first found it is not told.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The tale on the quays of Cuan shean

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The pilot of Ros bheag

events.title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg
events.body: Three crews from the western harbours bring word of the far land to the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, at Cathair dhearg. None claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three tellings; they agree on the coast and on nothing else.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Cuan shean crew heard in An Talla Dearg

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Ros bheag crew heard in An Talla Dearg

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Ceann mhòr crew heard in An Talla Dearg

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Murchadh's leaf of the three tellings

links.label: Leads to
links.title: How many days' water

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The ninth year of Queen Beathag

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill at nineteen

events.title: The Choosing
events.body: A vote, or what the later chroniclers call a vote, settles who will go. Only the willing go; no lots are drawn and none are pressed.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The question at the hearths

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Two households of Inis àrsaidh

links.label: At the same time
links.title: A custodian asks for the three tellings

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag at Cuan shean

events.title: The tale on the quays of Cuan shean
events.body: In the moon of Faolach the word of a far coast is on the quay at Cuan shean, told in the lee of the rope-sheds and at the crews' fire. No one says he saw the coast, and every telling leads back to another. By the moon's end it is told at Ros bheag, Inis àrsaidh and Ceann mhòr.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Land is found

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: II. Of a Word on the Quays

events.title: The pilot of Ros bheag
events.body: A pilot of Ros bheag, blown off the land in the autumn gales, comes home after nine days with his water gone. The coast shows up in the talk as his, but he swears he saw nothing but grey water, too loudly.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Land is found

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: II. Of a Word on the Quays

events.title: The Cuan shean crew heard in An Talla Dearg
events.body: Eachann mac Lachlainn, skipper of Cuan shean, tells the queen of a low dark coast west and north of west, with smoke on it and no hall. Asked if he was first to hear it, he says he was about the last.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: III. Of the Three Crews in the Red Hall

events.title: The Ros bheag crew heard in An Talla Dearg
events.body: Oighrig nic Raghnaill, skipper of Ros bheag, tells the queen that the coast lies north past the north cape, high and forested, with a white river, and that the pilot who saw it swore on the cup at Seann Skell.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: III. Of the Three Crews in the Red Hall

events.title: The Ceann mhòr crew heard in An Talla Dearg
events.body: Tòmas mac Uilleim of Ceann mhòr tells the queen that the land lies east behind the mist, and can be smelt on some mornings; the old men of the north-west have always said so.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: III. Of the Three Crews in the Red Hall

events.title: Murchadh's leaf of the three tellings
events.body: The queen's scribe Murchadh mac Eòghainn writes the three tellings on one leaf and adds at its foot that they agree on the coast and on nothing else. The leaf is kept in the chest of An Talla Dearg.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: III. Of the Three Crews in the Red Hall

events.title: How many days' water
events.body: At the lower board of An Talla Dearg the queen's sister Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill asks the Cuan shean skipper how many days' water a boat would need. He answers that no boat of the island could make the crossing, and that none has ever been built that could.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: IV. Of the Question at the Lower Board

events.title: The question at the hearths
events.body: Through the moon of Dubhlas the question 'Would we go?' is asked at hearths from Baile chrom to Seann Vell, most of all on the west coast. No lots are drawn and no lord or priest gives a word.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Choosing

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: V. Of the Choosing Begun

events.title: Two households of Inis àrsaidh
events.body: In the drying-shed at Inis àrsaidh two households say before the whole town that they will go if a boat is ever made that can make the crossing. The town laughs, then stops laughing.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Choosing

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: V. Of the Choosing Begun

events.title: A custodian asks for the three tellings
events.body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a young custodian of the western diggings, comes down to Cathair dhearg on an errand of Taigh na Fèithe and asks to hear the three tellings from the queen's scribe.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Choosing

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: V. Of the Choosing Begun

events.title: Mòrag at Cuan shean
events.body: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill rides alone to Cuan shean and questions Eachann mac Lachlainn on seams, winds and wood. He tells her a hull that needs no sewing would want great oak and a keel, and that no one alive knows how to set one.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Choosing

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: VI. Of Mòrag and the Skipper

events.title: The queen keeps the journey from the roll
events.body: Queen Beathag watches her sister walk the Cuan shean skipper to the gate of An Talla Dearg and look down the river road west. She bids Murchadh write nothing of it, since it is no matter for the roll yet.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The queen neither commands nor forbids

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: VII. Of the Queen at Her Window

events.title: The ninth year of Queen Beathag
events.body: An Talla Dearg's rolls enter the first year of the age as the ninth year of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, crowned at fifteen and now three-and-twenty: a good year for barley and a middling one for fish, with no child yet born to her.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: VIII. Of What Stood at the End of the Year

events.title: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill at nineteen
events.body: The queen's sister Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, nineteen years old and two years married to a man of the western shore she chose herself, comes up to the capital for the winter and sits at the lower board when the crews are heard.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Three Crews
told_in.section: IV. Of the Question at the Lower Board

events.title: The roll of the willing
events.body: The harbour scribes of Seann Skell open a roll of those who mean to go, written by household and not by name, on boards in the harbour-house. A later hand notes that names were struck out as often as they were added.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The first household asks to be written

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The rule of the whole household

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first striking-out

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A struck name is cut through

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The widow of the strand

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The late lamp in the harbour-house

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seonag asks the harbour scribe whether he would go

events.title: The queen neither commands nor forbids
events.body: Queen Beathag declares that the crown will send no one across the water and keep no one back. Within the season her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The queen keeps the journey from the roll

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dòmhnall mac Chaluim asks that the boards be closed

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The sisters in the bower

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The queen's word sent to the harbours

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The word read at the harbour-house door

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The queen's word made a song

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh says yes

events.title: The first household asks to be written
events.body: In the moon of Pailteach a fisher of Inis àrsaidh and his wife come into Taigh a' Chalaidh and ask to be written down as meaning to go. The harbour scribe Calum mac Nèill planes a new board and heads it: Those who mean to go.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The roll of the willing

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: II. Of the Opening of the Roll

events.title: The rule of the whole household
events.body: Calum mac Nèill will write a household whole or not at all, since Taigh na Fèithe measures the handful to the hearth and not to a single man or woman. The roll is kept by household from its first board.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The roll of the willing

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: III. Of the Rule of the Whole Household

events.title: The first striking-out
events.body: Iain, a net-maker of Seann Skell, strikes his household from the roll before the moon is out, having woken at night unable to breathe for thought of the open sea. He enters again in spring and strikes out again by midsummer.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The roll of the willing

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: V. Of the First Striking-Out

events.title: A struck name is cut through
events.body: Asked to scrape a struck name from the board, the harbour scribe refuses and cuts it through with one stroke, so that the roll shows both the meaning to go and the change of mind. The custom holds for every board of the roll.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The roll of the willing

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: V. Of the First Striking-Out

events.title: The widow of the strand
events.body: A boat-wright's widow of the Seann Skell strand is entered alone and struck three times over the first year, her name standing on the board three times like a ladder. She does not come back.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The roll of the willing

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: VI. Of the Widow of the Strand

events.title: The late lamp in the harbour-house
events.body: For those who cannot say it by day, Calum mac Nèill keeps a lamp burning in the harbour-house late into the night and pays for the oil himself. The harbour-house becomes a place between a court and a shrine.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The roll of the willing

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: VII. Of the Harbour-House at Night

events.title: Taigh na Fèithe sends to read the roll
events.body: A custodian's servant comes by night to read Rolla nan Deònach and ask how many households on it hold the right to the coal. From then on the harbour scribe marks each hearth that takes the handful with a notch like a flame.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians count the cost

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Waiting for a Word

events.title: Dòmhnall mac Chaluim asks that the boards be closed
events.body: The harbour scribe's son and clerk asks his father to close the roll and send the people to the queen. Calum will not close what the queen has not closed.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The queen neither commands nor forbids

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: IX. Of Dòmhnall mac Chaluim and the Closing of the Boards

events.title: Alasdair mac Iain reads the roll
events.body: A boat-wright of the strand, Alasdair mac Iain, reads every board of the roll and says there is not a boat on the island that could carry the half of them, and that somebody had better build one.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Alasdair Saor lays the first keel

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: X. Of the Question His Wife Asked

events.title: Seonag asks the harbour scribe whether he would go
events.body: Lying in the box-bed with the wind over the roof, Calum mac Nèill's wife Seonag, who keeps geese and sells their eggs on the quay, asks him whether he would go. He answers that the boards need a keeper.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The roll of the willing

told_in.book: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House
told_in.section: X. Of the Question His Wife Asked

events.title: The sisters in the bower
events.body: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill rides to Cathair dhearg and asks her sister to command or forbid the crossing. The queen answers that the crown has never sent anyone anywhere, nor kept back anyone free, and will not begin with her sister.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The queen neither commands nor forbids

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: I. Of the Bower in the Red Hall

events.title: The queen's word sent to the harbours
events.body: The queen's word, written by Murchadh mac Eòghainn and sealed, goes by rider to Seann Skell and every harbour of the west and to Taigh na Fèithe: the crown will send no one and keep no one back, and will judge any quarrel of the venture by the old law.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The queen neither commands nor forbids

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: II. Of the Word That Went Down the Road

events.title: The word read at the harbour-house door
events.body: Calum mac Nèill reads the queen's word twice from the harbour-house door to the town standing in the rain. Few cheer; most had wanted the crown to choose for them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The queen neither commands nor forbids

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: III. Of the Reading at the Door

events.title: The queen's word made a song
events.body: On the quay at Seann Skell the fishers say the queen's word over until it becomes a line of song: I will send no one over, and I will keep no one back. The harbour songs keep it so.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The queen neither commands nor forbids

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: III. Of the Reading at the Door

events.title: Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh says yes
events.body: At Inis àrsaidh Mòrag's husband, Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh, a farmer of the land up the river, agrees that their household will go before she has finished asking.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The queen neither commands nor forbids

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: IV. Of Aonghas at Inis àrsaidh

events.title: The custodians dispute the right of those who go
events.body: Through the winter the custodians at Taigh na Fèithe argue whether the right to the coal goes with a hearth that crosses the sea or is struck on the day it sails. Fearchar mac Ruairidh holds that the right lives in the hands.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The handful for the new hearth

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: VII. Of the Question of the Coal

events.title: The roll copied for Taigh na Fèithe
events.body: The harbour scribe's son copies Rolla nan Deònach onto skin, with a flame-mark beside each household that holds the right to the coal, and sends it up the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians count the cost

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Count Made Twice

events.title: Fearchar mac Ruairidh's household on the roll
events.body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh tells the custodians, after the second count, that he entered his own household on the roll at Seann Skell in the moon of Samhnas and ticked his own name twice.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians count the cost

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The willing choose their leaders

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: IX. Of Fearchar's Own Name

events.title: Nine days at the long table
events.body: In the moon of Lùghnas the custodians of Taigh na Fèithe sit at the long table with the copied roll on one side and Leabhar a' Chùraim on the other, and count hearth by hearth, name against name, for nine days.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians count the cost

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Count Made Twice

events.title: The custodians count the cost
events.body: The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, keeper of Crom's stone and heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal where Brìde's flame was first bound, counts the households of the coal-right that have entered the roll. The custody-book makes it nearly one in five, and says the count was made twice, for the first figure was not believed.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Taigh na Fèithe sends to read the roll

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The roll copied for Taigh na Fèithe

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Fearchar mac Ruairidh's household on the roll

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Nine days at the long table

events.title: Alasdair's small hulls
events.body: On the strand below Seann Skell the boat-wright Alasdair mac Iain builds hulls no longer than his arm on spines of oak and floats them in the river pool and the river mouth, to learn what a keel does. He finds that a keel makes a hull stiff and lets it be built bigger.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The ships are built

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: II. Of the Keel in the Tellings

events.title: Mòrag undertakes to pay for the oaks
events.body: At Inis àrsaidh Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh hear Alasdair out and send him to look at the grove of Doire fhionn. Mòrag undertakes to pay for the felling and hauling out of her own silver.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The oaks of Doire fhionn

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: III. Of the Lady at Inis àrsaidh

events.title: The ships are built
events.body: The shipwrights of the island, used to small coasting craft, build ships to keep the open sea, the first in the memory of Dia-thìr.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Alasdair's small hulls

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Woodcutters' huts at Doire fhiadhaich

events.title: Alasdair Saor lays the first keel
events.body: On the river strand below Seann Skell the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull built on Dia-thìr. Until then the island's boats were sewn-plank coasters that never lay a night out of sight of land.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Alasdair mac Iain reads the roll

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The bed of the first keel

events.title: The oaks of Doire fhionn
events.body: The oak grove that named Doire fhionn is felled for the keels of the fleet and drawn to the coast on ox-sleds. It never grew again, and the village kept a name it had no more cause for.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Mòrag undertakes to pay for the oaks

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The naming of the trees

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The felling of the Queen

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The ox-sleds on the north road

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Child walled

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Alasdair walks north with a knotted line

events.title: The shipwrights' fellowship
events.body: Alasdair Saor gathers the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into one fellowship, and binds each apprentice for seven years after the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book names it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Coinneach mac Fhearghais sworn

events.title: The naming of the trees
events.body: Eilidh nic Ruairidh, keeper of the grove of Doire fhionn, makes Alasdair choose each oak he will take and hear its name. He chooses fifty-four and leaves one young tree, the Child, standing alone.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The oaks of Doire fhionn

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: VI. Of the Naming of the Trees

events.title: The felling of the Queen
events.body: Eighty men of the households of the roll fell the grove of Doire fhionn through the summer, each tree onto a bed of brush. The greatest, called the Queen, takes two days to bring down.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The oaks of Doire fhionn

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: VII. Of the Felling

events.title: The ox-sleds on the north road
events.body: The keel-timbers are dragged forty-two miles south to the sea on sleds of oak shod with ash, six yoke to a sled. The road is widened at every bend and a causeway built over the stream below Doire fhionn.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The oaks of Doire fhionn

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Ox-Sleds on the North Road

events.title: Woodcutters' huts at Doire fhiadhaich
events.body: Woodcutters of the roll build huts at the edge of a wild oak wood on the shore of Loch chrom to fell crooked oak for the fleet's frames and knees. They go home when the felling is done and the huts fall in; the wood keeps its name.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ships are built

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Ox-Sleds on the North Road

events.title: The bed of the first keel
events.body: Alasdair levels a line of oak blocks on the strand above the high-water mark and digs a saw-pit beside it. The Queen oak is rolled onto the blocks and hewn to a keel with a ridge along its underside.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Alasdair Saor lays the first keel

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: IX. Of the First Keel

events.title: Coinneach mac Fhearghais sworn
events.body: At the feast of Lugh the wrights of the strand bind themselves into one fellowship. A custodian of Taigh na Fèithe swears their apprentices over a coal, and the first sworn is Coinneach mac Fhearghais, a coaster-wright's son of fourteen.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The shipwrights' fellowship

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: X. Of the Fellowship of the Strand

events.title: The first frames stand on the strand
events.body: By the moon of Pailteach the first frames rise from the keel in pairs, pegged with heart-oak. The harbour scribe writes that the hull looks like the ribs of a great beast picked clean on the shore.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: XI. Of the Frames Standing on the Strand

events.title: The Child walled
events.body: The village of Doire fhionn builds a low wall of stones round the one young oak left on the grove hill, and its old keeper sits beside it every evening until dark.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The oaks of Doire fhionn

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The coppice law of Doire fhionn

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: XI. Of the Frames Standing on the Strand

events.title: Alasdair walks north with a knotted line
events.body: In the moon of Gearras, after Là Fhèill Brìde, Alasdair mac Iain sets out alone on the north road with a pack, a staff and a line knotted every arm's length for measuring, making fifteen miles the first day and sleeping in a byre.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The oaks of Doire fhionn

told_in.book: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn
told_in.section: IV. Of the Road North

events.title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh
events.body: The first finished hull is taken down the Abhainn naomh and out past Ros àrsaidh, where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put to sea, for trial in open water. It founders in a following sea and eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor alters the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the new pattern.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The first frames stand on the strand

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Fhaoileag launched

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The nine named at Inis àrsaidh

links.title: The keening at Inis àrsaidh

links.title: Households struck and households entered

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The second keel laid to the changed pattern

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Dara Fhaoileag planked

events.title: An Fhaoileag launched
events.body: The first deep-keeled hull, planked and rigged, is floated off the blocks below Seann Skell with a coal from Taigh na Fèithe set at her step. The town calls her An Fhaoileag, the gull, for the way she rides the water.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: I. Of the Launching of An Fhaoileag

events.title: The nine named at Inis àrsaidh
events.body: The roll-keeper of Inis àrsaidh cuts eleven names into the village's board on the night of the drowning, the village sitting up with her as the custom asks. Alasdair's sister's son Tormod Beag is among the eight bodies brought back; three more are never found.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: III. Of the Names Cut at Inis àrsaidh

events.title: The keening at Inis àrsaidh
events.body: The eight recovered dead are keened on the shingle under sailcloth and a lamp at each head; for the three never found a single lamp is lit and burns down unwatched. Alasdair stays three days doing whatever the village asks of him.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: III. Of the Names Cut at Inis àrsaidh

events.title: Households struck and households entered
events.body: Eleven households strike themselves from the Seann Skell roll after word of the drowning, and eleven others enter in the same weeks, among them kin of a survivor and a widow of Ros bheag who gives her daughters' names. Calum mac Nèill records both counts without comment.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: VI. Of Those Who Struck Themselves Out, and Those Who Entered

events.title: The second keel laid to the changed pattern
events.body: Alasdair Saor lays a second keel on the strand below Seann Skell, built to the fuller, hollow-bowed run he redrew by a driftwood fire after the drowning. Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill sends silver again to see her built.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: V. Of the Second Keel

events.title: The rope-walks of Cuan shean
events.body: Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and gives all its hemp fields to cordage for the fleet. Its rope trade lasts some centuries beyond the Sundering.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The rope-walks learn the names of a keel

events.title: The rope-walks learn the names of a keel
events.body: After shroud-lines sent west from Cuan shean fail within a season, the wrights walk the rope-walks and name the parts of a hull to the spinners and walkers. Iain Ròpaire, master of the walks, takes to walking one himself to learn the words in his own hands.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The rope-walks of Cuan shean

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: VII. Of the Rope-Walks of Cuan shean

events.title: Birth of Raghnall mac Uilleim
events.body: A son, Raghnall, is born at Cathair dhearg to Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill and her consort Uilleam mac Iain, in the queen's sixteenth year crowned and her own thirtieth year of life.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Death of Queen Beathag

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: V. Of the Second Keel

events.title: The sail-cloth levy
events.body: Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh owes a set length of close-woven sail-cloth, scored on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many paid is not known.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The sail-cloth tallies at Baile àrsaidh

events.title: The sail-cloth tallies at Baile àrsaidh
events.body: The shire seat's tally-keeper cuts notches for close-woven lengths from households across Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh, far more than expected, some sent by weavers with no kin on the roll and no thought of sailing. The sticks fill a chest that wants a second lid.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The sail-cloth levy

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Sail-Cloth of Baile àrsaidh

events.title: An Dara Fhaoileag planked
events.body: An Dara Fhaoileag stands planked from keel to sheer and steps her mast on the strand below Seann Skell. The wrights name her An Dara Fhaoileag, the second gull, and the doubt among the older wrights over her fuller, hollow-bowed lines goes quiet.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh

told_in.book: Of the Hull that Lay Down
told_in.section: IX. Of the Hull that Stood Beside Her Sister

events.title: Six pilots sent east to Cuan ruadh
events.body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh finds that no pilot of the west coast has ever held a course by night, and six are chosen to walk the hundred miles to the old steersmen of Cuan ruadh: two of Ceann mhòr, two of Ros bheag, one of Cuan shean, and Catrìona nic Iain, who asks to be sent before she is asked.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh
told_in.section: I. Of the Six Who Went East

events.title: The six pilots reach Cuan ruadh
events.body: After seven days on foot over the mountain country the six pilots come down to Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast and are given lodging without question. They are sent, the next morning, to the steersman Seumas Reultach.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh
told_in.section: I. Of the Six Who Went East

events.title: Seumas Reultach begins the teaching
events.body: On the headland above Cuan ruadh the old steersman Seumas Reultach begins teaching the six pilots the wheel of the sky and Reul na Stiùire, by which it is held. Most of what he gives them is spoken, night after night, and set down nowhere.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh
told_in.section: II. Of the Steersman of Cuan ruadh

events.title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh
events.body: The old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night, teach the pilots of the fleet to steer by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part is lost.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Six pilots sent east to Cuan ruadh

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The six pilots reach Cuan ruadh

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Seumas Reultach begins the teaching

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Part of the star-lore set on hide

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Death of Seumas Reultach

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The pilots return west

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first night-steering trial off Ros àrsaidh

events.title: Part of the star-lore set on hide
events.body: At Taigh na Fèithe's asking, Seumas Reultach has his granddaughter cut onto a scraped hide the wheel of the sky, Reul na Stiùire and the four turning marks of the year. He keeps back the swell-reading and the wind-smell, saying some things a hide can hold and some things only a life can.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh
told_in.section: II. Of the Steersman of Cuan ruadh

events.title: Death of Seumas Reultach
events.body: In the moon of Faolach the old steersman of Cuan ruadh dies on the cliff path above the town where he taught the six pilots the stars, and is buried there among his own people. His granddaughter gives the hide of star-marks into Catrìona nic Iain's keeping to carry west.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh
told_in.section: II. Of the Steersman of Cuan ruadh

events.title: The pilots return west
events.body: The six pilots cross the mountain country again to the west coast, carrying the hide of star-marks and what they have learned of the wheel of the sky, Reul na Stiùire and the smell of the dark before a change of wind.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh
told_in.section: II. Of the Steersman of Cuan ruadh

events.title: The first night-steering trial off Ros àrsaidh
events.body: Off Ros àrsaidh two boats go out after dark, one steered close along the shore by lantern, the other by Catrìona nic Iain alone by Reul na Stiùire with every lantern doused. She brings her boat home first, exactly where and when she had said she would.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh
told_in.section: III. Of the First Trial and the Star Named on the Quay

events.title: Catrìona nic Iain made pilot of An Ròn Glas
events.body: Catrìona nic Iain reaches Seann Skell after the households of the roll have chosen Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and Fearchar mac Ruairidh to lead them. On the west quay Mòrag asks her to be pilot of her hull, An Ròn Glas, and Catrìona names her Reul na Stiùire.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The willing choose their leaders

told_in.book: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh
told_in.section: III. Of the First Trial and the Star Named on the Quay

events.title: The willing choose their leaders
events.body: The households of the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein, to lead them. The custody-book records the choice; how it was made is not told.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Fearchar mac Ruairidh's household on the roll

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Catrìona nic Iain made pilot of An Ròn Glas

events.title: Fearchar's petition for the coal
events.body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh comes to Taigh na Fèithe and asks that each hull found fit to sail be allowed to carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household's season under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig. The custodians send him down the hill with a promise only to put the matter to the board.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The handful for the new hearth

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: II. Of the Petition

events.title: Donnchadh mac Thormoid given to Taigh na Fèithe
events.body: Tormod, a turf-cutter of the moor above Muileann dhearg, walks his son Donnchadh, nine years old, up the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe and leaves him there sworn to the vein's service for seven years, and does not look back.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The handful for the new hearth

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: I. Of the Boy Given to the Vein-House

events.title: The handful for the new hearth
events.body: The vein-house rules that each departing ship may carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. It is the only writing in the custody-book addressed to those who were leaving.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The custodians dispute the right of those who go

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Fearchar's petition for the coal

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Donnchadh mac Thormoid given to Taigh na Fèithe

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians' debate at the winter burning

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The sealed measures made

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fair copy of the ruling, Donnchadh's first entry

events.title: The custodians' debate at the winter burning
events.body: After six winters of argument Taigh na Fèithe's board finally votes on Fearchar's petition. Cailean and others hold that the coal has never crossed water and should not; Fearchar answers that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig measures a hearth wherever a hearth chooses to stand. Leabhar a' Chùraim is opened and the question is put to writing.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The handful for the new hearth

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: III. Of the Winter Burning

events.title: The sealed measures made
events.body: The first measures of coal are weighed and sealed at Taigh na Fèithe, each against the words "for each hull that shall be ready", with no count kept against any known number of hulls. Fearchar mac Ruairidh stands by in silence to see the first one made.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The handful for the new hearth

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: V. Of the Measures Sealed

events.title: The queen lends masons for the quay
events.body: Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill sends a gang of masons from the capital, under Ailean mac Nèill, down to Seann Skell to lengthen the west quay with dressed stone "for the harbour's trade", the crown's word for it and no other named.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The west quay lengthened

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: VI. Of the Masons Sent West

events.title: The fair copy of the ruling, Donnchadh's first entry
events.body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the boy-clerk, is set at fifteen to render the ruling clean for Leabhar a' Chùraim, after it has lain four years in rough marks: one sealed measure a ship, a single household's season, Taigh na Fèithe's own mark. He copies it exactly as given, though he notices it carries no blessing, as other entries do.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The handful for the new hearth

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: IV. Of the Clean Copy

events.title: The queen at Seann Skell to see the stones laid
events.body: Beathag rides the twenty-four miles to Seann Skell and stands on the new-laid stone of the west quay in the evening light, the only time she is known to have come to see the fleet's building with her own eyes. Her sister Mòrag joins her there, and the two speak of small things, not of the roll.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The west quay lengthened

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: VII. Of the Queen on the New Stones

events.title: Death of Uilleam mac Iain, the queen's consort
events.body: Uilleam mac Iain, husband to Queen Beathag and father of her son, dies after a summer's illness. The queen keeps the funeral small, a single day at Cathair dhearg with the household and a few custodian heads, and no great muster of the shires.

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Death of Uilleam mac Iain

events.title: The west quay lengthened
events.body: Masons from the capital lengthen the west quay at Seann Skell with dressed stone, so that the deep hulls may lie alongside at low water. On these stones the later rite was held.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The queen lends masons for the quay

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The queen at Seann Skell to see the stones laid

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The iron cramp of the last stone

events.title: Death of Eòghann mac Mhuirich
events.body: The master of Taigh na Fèithe, who wrote the first count of the departing households in LE 3, dies at Taigh na Fèithe grown very old, soon after seeing the ruling of the coal for the departing set down and its first measures sealed.

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: I. Of the Boy Given to the Vein-House

events.title: The iron cramp of the last stone
events.body: Ailean mac Nèill's gang sets the last stone of the lengthened quay at the seaward end, where the new masonry meets the old timber staging, and Ailean drives home the iron cramp that binds them with three blows and no more.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The west quay lengthened

told_in.book: Of the Handful for the New Hearth
told_in.section: IX. Of the Last Stone and the Sealing by Lamplight

events.title: Tormod mac Coinnich remembers the dearth of his boyhood
events.body: As the council weighs how much grain the fleet may take, the reeve of the granaries at Àth shean turns over an old memory: a reeve before him who smiled and gave no grain, and a store-house that stood swept and empty a whole hungry spring. He resolves that his own stores will not be opened on a smile.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Àth shean shuts its granaries

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: II. Of the Barred Doors

events.title: A lean harvest in the south shires
events.body: The barley comes in thin across the shires south of the mountain, the fourth-poorest harvest in eleven years by the granary reeve's own tallies. The stores at Àth shean, well kept, would see the country through to spring, but word soon comes that the fleet's crossing must be fed from them too.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The strife over the grain

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: I. Of the Lean Harvest

events.title: The council of An Talla Dearg divided on the grain
events.body: Through the autumn the queen's council argues over how much stored grain the departing may carry, some holding that no household should cross open water without bread enough, others that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was never meant to measure a granary. The queen gives no opinion any rider carries south.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The strife over the grain

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: II. Of the Barred Doors

events.title: Petitioners come to the barred granary
events.body: With no ruling yet come from the capital, petitioners for the fleet's stores gather at Tormod mac Coinnich's door at Àth shean on no authority he can name. He bars the store-house doors and sets a watch of four, and turns away captain's steward and quiet petitioner alike until the council's own seal comes down.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Àth shean shuts its granaries

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: II. Of the Barred Doors

events.title: The watch stands through the winter
events.body: Four men keep the granary doors at Àth shean through Samhnas and Dubhlas and the black months after, relieved every third day, while riders come from the capital with sealed leaves that settle nothing. Tormod mac Coinnich walks the round with them most nights, unable to say when, or whether, the matter will be settled.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Àth shean shuts its granaries

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: II. Of the Barred Doors

events.title: The strife over the grain
events.body: Strife over how much of the island's stored grain the ships may take all but ends the venture. Within a season it is settled; how is not recorded.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: A lean harvest in the south shires

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The council of An Talla Dearg divided on the grain

events.title: Àth shean shuts its granaries
events.body: In the strife over the fleet's grain Tormod mac Coinnich, reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them until the matter is settled. He holds no office afterward.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Tormod mac Coinnich remembers the dearth of his boyhood

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Petitioners come to the barred granary

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The watch stands through the winter

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The granary doors reopened

events.title: Grain down Abhainn dhomhain
events.body: The strife settled, grain barges go down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital, on by the coast to Ros àrsaidh, and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts forty-one barges passing.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The granary doors reopened

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mairead nic Iain's tally of the barges

events.title: The fleet assembled
events.body: The fleet lies complete at Seann Skell. The custody-book gives nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin makes it twenty-one. Which is right has never been settled.

links.label: Same place
links.title: Calum's daughter's household entered

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fleet's stores laid in at Seann Skell

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Niall mac Dhòmhnaill counts the hulls and loses count

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The queen walks the new quay at Seann Skell

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The queen and her sister on the stones

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The queen rides home before the sailing

events.title: The granary doors reopened
events.body: A single rider comes to Àth shean with no sealed leaf, only a word that the grain may move at a fixed measure. Tormod mac Coinnich takes the bar down himself and calls off the watch; how the strife was settled, and by whom, he is never told. He holds no office after, and walks home to his father's farm.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Àth shean shuts its granaries

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Grain down Abhainn dhomhain

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: III. Of the Doors Reopened

events.title: Mairead nic Iain's tally of the barges
events.body: On Drochaid Cathair dhearg the tally-keeper Mairead nic Iain cuts a notch in a hazel stick for every laden barge that passes beneath, going down Abhainn dhomhain toward the coast. When the season's grain has all gone by she makes the count forty-one, and writes it down with no more comment than that.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Grain down Abhainn dhomhain

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: IV. Of the Forty-One Barges

events.title: Calum's daughter's household entered
events.body: At Taigh a' Chalaidh, Calum mac Nèill cuts his own daughter's household onto Rolla nan Deònach: Mairead nic Chaluim, her husband Dùghall mac Iain, a fisher of Inis àrsaidh, and their two small children. His son Dòmhnall sets the cup of ale in his sister's hands, and Calum's hand shakes only once the harbour-house stands empty again.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The fleet assembled

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: V. Of the Roll at Seann Skell

events.title: The fleet's stores laid in at Seann Skell
events.body: The grain that came down Abhainn dhomhain and up the Abhainn naomh is measured out and sealed aboard the hulls at Seann Skell against the fleet's crossing, one measure to a household under Taigh na Fèithe's own ruling. By spring the quay stands full of hulls that had not existed when the first tale of a far shore reached the river road.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fleet assembled

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: II. Of the Barred Doors

events.title: Niall mac Dhòmhnaill counts the hulls and loses count
events.body: Calum's grandson Niall, nine years old, runs the length of the new quay after his lessons, touching each hull's timbers as he passes and trying, unasked, to count the whole fleet. He never once brings the count out even, and a wright who helped lay four of the hulls tells him he could not have done better himself.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The fleet assembled

told_in.book: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges
told_in.section: VI. Of the Hulls at the Quay

events.title: The queen walks the new quay at Seann Skell
events.body: In the moon of Sìolach, Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill comes down to Seann Skell with a small household and walks the whole length of the new stone quay at the harbour scribe's side, saying little, before finding her sister on the strand below.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fleet assembled

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: I. Of the Queen on the New Stones

events.title: The queen and her sister on the stones
events.body: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill comes up from the rope-maker's gear to meet her sister on the new stones. What passes between them is not told; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives only that the queen was seen upon the quay with her sister, and went home again before the sailing, as her own word bound her to do.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fleet assembled

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: I. Of the Queen on the New Stones

events.title: The queen rides home before the sailing
events.body: Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill leaves Seann Skell the same evening she comes to it, telling the harbour scribe she will not be at the quay for the sailing itself, for a queen who has sworn to send no one over and keep no one back has no cause to watch her own sister taken by that same promise.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fleet assembled

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: I. Of the Queen on the New Stones

events.title: The night of lamps
events.body: On the last night before the sailing every house on the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning till morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering written down as a custom, and the town kept it long after its cause had become a tale.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Niall given the counting-stick

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The lamps lit unasked along the strand

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mairead nic Chaluim's household goes aboard

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag walks the waterfront alone

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Catrìona takes the steering oar of An Ròn Glas

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Fionnlagh stands by his cart and does not go

events.title: The Setting-Out
events.body: The willing sail out past the north cape. The chronicles of the island fall silent on them as the ships clear the harbour; the Dia-thìrich tell that the fleet sailed into Manannan's mist, toward the Otherworld.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The queen hears a boundary plea on the morning of the sailing

events.title: Niall given the counting-stick
events.body: On the eve of the sailing Calum mac Nèill gives his grandson Niall, eleven years old, a shaved hazel stick and a knife, and sets him on the wall of the west quay to cut one notch for every hull that passes in the morning, with the single instruction to keep his eyes on the count and not on the faces.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night of lamps

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: II. Of the Lamps on the Sills

events.title: The lamps lit unasked along the strand
events.body: Beginning at one widow's window by the fish-stones, a lamp is set on every sill along the Seann Skell waterfront the evening before the sailing, and kept burning until morning, though no one has told the town to do it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night of lamps

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: II. Of the Lamps on the Sills

events.title: Mairead nic Chaluim's household goes aboard
events.body: Calum mac Nèill's daughter Mairead, her husband Dùghall mac Iain and their two children take their places aboard their hull on the eve of the sailing, their stores lashed under oiled hide; Mairead asks a deep notch cut for her hull, whichever number it falls at.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night of lamps

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: II. Of the Lamps on the Sills

events.title: Mòrag walks the waterfront alone
events.body: On the last night Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill walks the length of the Seann Skell strand twice over, naming to herself the household behind every lit window, a leave-taking asked of no one and told to no one beforehand.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night of lamps

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: III. Of Mòrag's Last Walk

events.title: Catrìona takes the steering oar of An Ròn Glas
events.body: Aboard An Ròn Glas on the eve of the sailing, the pilot Catrìona nic Iain tells Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill that the oar answers well and the ship rides true, whatever else the morning brings.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night of lamps

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: III. Of Mòrag's Last Walk

events.title: Fionnlagh stands by his cart and does not go
events.body: A carter of Seann Skell named Fionnlagh, who has brought loads down to the quay for departing households all that season without putting his own name to the boards, stands by his empty cart through Oidhche nan Lòchran and through the sailing itself, and does not go aboard any hull.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night of lamps

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: III. Of Mòrag's Last Walk

events.title: Niall's tally of An Diosal
events.body: On the morning of the sailing Niall mac Dhòmhnaill cuts one notch on his hazel stick for every hull that passes the west quay wall going round the river pool sunwise, and keeps the finished stick inside his shirt afterward; no one ever asks him for it back.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The sunwise turn

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: IV. Of the Sunwise Turn

events.title: The queen hears a boundary plea on the morning of the sailing
events.body: At Cathair dhearg, on the same morning the fleet turns out of Seann Skell, Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill hears an ordinary dispute between two farmers over a shifted boundary ditch and rules it with the same care she gives any such matter, no rider from the coast yet able to have reached her.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Setting-Out

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: V. Of the Boundary Ditch

events.title: The empty berths walked that evening
events.body: That evening Calum mac Nèill walks the whole length of the west quay and finds the berths standing empty for the first time in three years, and tells his son Dòmhnall that a harbour built for nothing but to be full is a strange thing to walk when it stands empty.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The sunwise turn

told_in.book: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn
told_in.section: V. Of the Boundary Ditch

events.title: The sunwise turn
events.body: Before going down the Abhainn naomh to the open sea the fleet goes once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The harbour scribe's account ends at the foot of the pool.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Niall's tally of An Diosal

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The empty berths walked that evening

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Leabhar a' Chùraim's entry of the turn

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Death of Calum mac Nèill, Niall takes the harbour-house

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Niall keeps his grandfather's stick at his own elbow

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Death of Niall mac Dhòmhnaill

events.title: Leabhar a' Chùraim's entry of the turn
events.body: At Taigh na Fèithe Donnchadh mac Thormoid enters the turn of the fleet into Leabhar a' Chùraim under a day after Samhain, a full turning of the moon and more after every other account sets the sailing itself. The gap between the two dates is copied faithfully and explained by no word in the leaf that reaches him.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The sunwise turn

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: I. Of the Entry a Day Too Late

events.title: The years counted from the turn
events.body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes take it up a generation later.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Donnchadh begins Bliadhnaichean an Diosail

events.title: Tidings reach Seann Skell
events.body: Tidings of the fleet reach Seann Skell, by what road or whose mouth is not told. The harbour scribe copies them in a shaking hand; the copy came down to later keepers water-stained and lacking its end.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Broken tidings come to the harbour-house

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The tidings copied to An Talla Dearg and Taigh na Fèithe

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The tale kept two ways at once at Inis àrsaidh

events.title: Two landfalls
events.body: Such broken tidings as come back tell of two coasts reached, not one. In this telling lies the seed of the two peoples that came after.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Two shores, not one

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council divided over the two shores

events.title: Donnchadh begins Bliadhnaichean an Diosail
events.body: For his own ledger's convenience, and for no reason he offers anyone, Taigh na Fèithe clerk Donnchadh mac Thormoid begins to number years from An Diosal rather than from a reign, working the count backward through his private book to the turn itself. No one above him asks him to keep it, and he tells no one that he does.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The years counted from the turn

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: II. Of the Years of the Diosal

events.title: Broken tidings come to the harbour-house
events.body: Word of the fleet reaches Seann Skell by a boat that does not stay to be questioned. Calum mac Nèill copies the telling that same night in a shaking hand; the letters run smaller toward the leaf's foot, and the copy stops without warning where the telling itself stopped.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Tidings reach Seann Skell

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: III. Of the Tidings that Reached Seann Skell

events.title: Two shores, not one
events.body: Calum's leaf tells of two separate landfalls reached by hulls that had not held together the whole crossing, whether by storm, purpose, or a quarrel the telling does not say. It gives no word of which households reached which shore, and its torn end settles nothing.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Two landfalls

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: III. Of the Tidings that Reached Seann Skell

events.title: The tidings copied to An Talla Dearg and Taigh na Fèithe
events.body: A fair copy of Calum's leaf goes by rider to Cathair dhearg for the queen's own council; a second copy, made by his son Dòmhnall, goes east to Taigh na Fèithe, where Donnchadh mac Thormoid sets it beside his own four-year-old entry of the turn and finds the silence between them unexplained by either leaf.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Tidings reach Seann Skell

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: V. Of the Copy that Went by Two Roads

events.title: The council divided over the two shores
events.body: At An Talla Dearg the custodians argue whether two landfalls mean the fleet prospered or was scattered, and which of the nineteen or one-and-twenty hulls reached which coast. Queen Beathag hears the whole of it and says nothing, and the council lets the matter drop for the day's ordinary business.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Two landfalls

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: V. Of the Copy that Went by Two Roads

events.title: The tale kept two ways at once at Inis àrsaidh
events.body: The broken telling of two shores reaches the fishing hearths of Inis àrsaidh, which gave more households to the roll than any other place. With no way to know which shore holds which kin, the town keeps both halves of the tale alive together, grieving toward one and hoping toward the other by turns.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Tidings reach Seann Skell

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: IV. Of the Hearths of Inis àrsaidh

events.title: Birth of Raghnall mac Raghnaill
events.body: A son, named for his father, is born at Cathair dhearg to Raghnall mac Uilleim, the queen's heir, then seven-and-thirty years old. The boy is Beathag's first grandson and the third of her line under An Talla Dearg's roof.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: V. Of the Copy that Went by Two Roads

events.title: Mòrag's line struck
events.body: Queen Beathag strikes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the succession, as no longer on Dia-thìr. The act stands without comment between a grain ruling and the mending of a bridge.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag's line struck in the ordinary hand

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Murchadh sands the leaf

events.title: The grain ruling settled
events.body: A long dispute over grain owed the crown's granaries by the upland shires is settled in the queen's favour, the reeves agreeing at last to a measure put to them in her own hand rather than a steward's.

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: VI. Of the Grain Ruling and the Bridge

events.title: The bridge at Àth shean mended in stone
events.body: The cracked middle pier of the bridge at Àth shean, shored with timber since a flood two winters before, is rebuilt in stone by masons from the capital, the last props pulled clear on a morning cold enough to break the river's ice.

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: VI. Of the Grain Ruling and the Bridge

events.title: Mòrag's line struck in the ordinary hand
events.body: Between the grain ruling and the bridge, in the same plain hand as either, the queen has Murchadh mac Eòghainn enter that Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and her children are struck from the succession, as persons no longer on Dia-thìr. Only the old scribe's pen slows at the shaping of the name.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Mòrag's line struck

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: VII. Of the Name Written the Ordinary Way

events.title: Murchadh sands the leaf
events.body: Alone in the near-emptied hall, old Murchadh mac Eòghainn sands the leaf that struck the queen's sister from the roll, the same practised motion he has closed every entry with for forty years, giving away nothing of what lies written beneath the sand.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Mòrag's line struck

told_in.book: Of the Count from the Turn
told_in.section: V. Of the Copy that Went by Two Roads

events.title: The taproom tales of An Tanachadh at Seann Skell
events.body: A coal-carrier's widow tells at the harbour-house that the children born to the departed on the far shore carry less in their hands than their parents did, and less again by the third generation. A custodian down from Taigh na Fèithe answers her over a jug that the coal was never carried in the blood at all, only left behind at Muileann dhearg like a tool in an unvisited shed. Neither tale is tried against anything Seann Skell holds.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The thinning

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: I. Of What Was Said at Seann Skell

events.title: A third telling that silences a room
events.body: A telling heard less often than the other two at Seann Skell holds that nothing thins at all: the far shore never had the coal to answer to, so its children are unremarked only for want of anything to remark them against. It is told least of the three, though it silences a hearth where the others merely fill one.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The thinning

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: I. Of What Was Said at Seann Skell

events.title: The rite named an Tùrsa Geal
events.body: The court names the queen's mourning an Tùrsa Geal, and within a generation any household on the island that gave someone to the fleet keeps some form of the same rite unasked, undyed wool and an empty place laid with cup, trencher and straight knife, needing no crown or law behind it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The white sorrow first kept at court

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: III. Of the White Sorrow

events.title: The thinning
events.body: Cut off from the vein, the strength the crossing asked of them fades in the children of those who went. By the third generation over the water nothing is left that Dia-thìr would know.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The taproom tales of An Tanachadh at Seann Skell

links.label: At the same time
links.title: A third telling that silences a room

events.title: The custodians' second count
events.body: The vein-house counts again the households of the coal-right and sets the loss at one hand in five. Beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein answers no differently for those who stayed.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Taigh na Fèithe's second count made

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Donnchadh's note that the vein answers no differently

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Beathag reads the second count twice

events.title: Taigh na Fèithe's second count made
events.body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now nine-and-thirty, carries the greater share of Taigh na Fèithe's second tallying, checking Rolla nan Deònach against the coal-right's remaining hearths column by column. The count stands where the first count of the roll had stood: one hearth in five gone from the coal-right, no more and no fewer than had sailed.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The custodians' second count

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: II. Of the Second Count

events.title: Donnchadh's note that the vein answers no differently
events.body: Beneath the count Donnchadh mac Thormoid sets a second line unasked: that the vein answers no differently now to the hands of those who stayed than it answered before the turn, and that whatever thins in the departed's children thins on their own shore, not on this side of the water. It is carried up to Cathair dhearg with the season's reckoning.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The custodians' second count

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: II. Of the Second Count

events.title: Beathag reads the second count twice
events.body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill reads Taigh na Fèithe's figure of one hand in five, a number she has carried unwritten in her own reckoning since the fleet sailed, and reads Donnchadh's note beneath it a second time more slowly than the first. She sets the leaf down in its place among the season's ordinary business and says no more of it that day.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The custodians' second count

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: II. Of the Second Count

events.title: The queen first wears the undyed wool
events.body: Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill comes into An Talla Dearg in plain undyed wool for the first time in more than fifty years of reigning in the deep blue of the house of Dòmhnall, and takes up the day's first petition as though nothing were changed, giving the court no word for it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The white sorrow first kept at court

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: III. Of the White Sorrow

events.title: The empty place first laid at the queen's table
events.body: Beathag lays a cup, a trencher and a straight knife at the foot of her own table each evening she dines in hall, mourning her sister Mòrag with no grave to stand at and no body to wash. The court, told by the queen's steward that she mourns a sister ten years and more beyond any word reaching Cathair dhearg, does not know at first whether to speak of the place or pass it in silence.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The white sorrow first kept at court

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: III. Of the White Sorrow

events.title: The Mourning Custom
events.body: Dia-thìr sets in order a rite of mourning for the departed, neither wholly grief nor wholly feast. In a far later age it was used again, uneasily, for a very different leaving.

events.title: The white sorrow first kept at court
events.body: Queen Beathag mourns her sister in undyed wool, with one place left empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and within a generation it is kept in every harbour town of the island.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The rite named an Tùrsa Geal

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The queen first wears the undyed wool

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The empty place first laid at the queen's table

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The empty place laid once more at the queen's wake

events.title: Donnchadh speaks of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's limit
events.body: At a sitting of Taigh na Fèithe called for another matter, Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now its senior clerk, says plainly that the old apprenticeship built for the numbers before the turn has gone as far as the older custodians' own stretching can carry it, and that Taigh na Fèithe owes itself an honest look at what remains.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians fewer

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: IV. Of the Seven Houses

events.title: The sitting on the seven kindreds argued two days
events.body: A custodian of a small old name that kept a single gallery for three generations speaks bitterly against folding his household's right into a larger kindred. An old woman of Clann Thormoid, who has buried a brother and two nephews to the roll, answers that she would sooner see her right folded into a house that can still walk its galleries than stand alone over ones it cannot serve, and the sitting turns on her answer.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians fewer

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The seven houses of custody

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: IV. Of the Seven Houses

events.title: The custodians fewer
events.body: With part of the coal-bound folk gone, the Dia-thìrich order themselves anew about a smaller and closer class of custodians. From this shape every later nobility descends.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Donnchadh speaks of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's limit

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The sitting on the seven kindreds argued two days

events.title: The seven houses of custody
events.body: The custodian households that remain are gathered into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the coal and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Here for the first time the right to the coal passes by house and not by apprenticeship.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The sitting on the seven kindreds argued two days

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Na Seachd Taighean sworn

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Donnchadh writes Mionnan nan Seachd heads

events.title: Death of Queen Beathag
events.body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Dia-thìr who saw the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Birth of Raghnall mac Uilleim

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Death of Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill at seventy-six

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Raghnall mac Uilleim crowned at seven-and-forty

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The empty place laid once more at the queen's wake

events.title: Na Seachd Taighean sworn
events.body: Taigh na Fèithe gathers the remaining custodian households into seven kindreds large enough to answer for a share of the galleries between them: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Their seven heads are sworn before Crom's stone, and the right to the coal passes from that year by house and no longer by apprenticeship alone.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The seven houses of custody

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: IV. Of the Seven Houses

events.title: Donnchadh writes Mionnan nan Seachd heads
events.body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid enters the seven heads' oath into Leabhar a' Chùraim in the same plain hand he has kept his whole working life, and finds himself thinking less of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig than of the fifth of hands the sitting never once named aloud: those fifteen years and a whole sea away, on a shore the book has no line to enter them against.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The seven houses of custody

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: IV. Of the Seven Houses

events.title: Death of Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill at seventy-six
events.body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg in the summer, seventy and six years old, after one-and-sixty years upon An Talla Dearg's floor, the oldest of her line and the last ruler who saw the fleet built and sent. She holds a boundary petition to its ordinary end that same morning before going to her rooms and not rising again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Death of Queen Beathag

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: V. Of the Crowning at Cathair dhearg

events.title: Raghnall mac Uilleim crowned at seven-and-forty
events.body: Raghnall mac Uilleim, son of Beathag and of Uilleam mac Iain, is crowned in An Talla Dearg within the month of his mother's death, seven-and-forty years old and long seated at her board. He wears a strip of undyed wool beneath his crowning colours, a thing he grew up watching his mother wear and never asked leave to wear himself.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Death of Queen Beathag

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: V. Of the Crowning at Cathair dhearg

events.title: The empty place laid once more at the queen's wake
events.body: At the second night of Beathag's wake her steward lays the cup, trencher and straight knife once more at the foot of her table exactly as she always kept them, so that the court, passing between the small emptiness at the board's foot and the greater one at the board's head, cannot say with certainty whether the place is laid for the queen or still for the sister she mourned fifteen years across an unanswering sea.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Death of Queen Beathag

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The white sorrow first kept at court

told_in.book: Of the White Sorrow
told_in.section: VI. Of the Empty Place Laid Once More

events.title: Murchadh mac Raghnaill takes the berths
events.body: The harbour-master of Seann Skell retires to his daughter's house up the Abhainn naomh rather than die at his post, and Murchadh mac Raghnaill, of an age with Niall mac Dhòmhnaill, takes the berths and the dues.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The harbour at half trade

told_in.book: Of the Empty Harbour
told_in.section: III. Of the Harbour at Half Trade

events.title: Death of Calum mac Nèill, Niall takes the harbour-house
events.body: Calum mac Nèill, harbour scribe of Seann Skell for six-and-fifty years, dies in the room above the harbour-house. The boards pass, as he had let the town see coming, to his grandson Niall mac Dhòmhnaill, the boy who once counted the hulls with a hazel stick, now a man of nine-and-twenty.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The sunwise turn

told_in.book: Of the Empty Harbour
told_in.section: I. Of the Boards Given Over

events.title: Dòmhnall mac Chaluim keeps the trade rolls
events.body: Passed over for the boards he had expected, Calum's son Dòmhnall keeps the harbour-house's trade rolls and dues, working the office beside his own son Niall without open quarrel, though he calls the boards the queerest inheritance a man could be passed over for.

told_in.book: Of the Empty Harbour
told_in.section: I. Of the Boards Given Over
