events.body: When the snow that trapped a party of reeves at An Taigh-seinnse Reòta finally lifts, the house's keeper sends after them, by the first cart through, a bill for every jar of pickled spinach and every cup of fire milk they took, itemised, and it is paid in full.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: II. Of the Houses on the Circuit

events.title: The hull that sank at launch
events.body: Seumas mac Iain, a boat-builder of Seann Skell, tries to build a deep-keeled hull again from the scraps of the Sundering fellowship's lore still remembered on the strand. At its launch it fills and sinks, and Manannan's priests preach on it for a year.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seumas mac Iain gives up the deep keel

events.title: Seumas mac Iain gives up the deep keel
events.body: After a year of Manannan's priests preaching against his sunken hull, the boat-builder of Seann Skell builds no more deep keels, and keeps his harbour shed mending ordinary boats for ordinary fares until his death.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hull that sank at launch

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: III. Of the Hull That Filled

events.title: The Caol ìseal fishers go east
events.body: Their own harbour silted, the fishing families of Caol ìseal on the north coast move east to Caol bheag. Caol ìseal becomes a farming town.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The shrine carried whole to Caol bheag

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Caol ìseal turns to the plough

events.title: The shrine carried whole to Caol bheag
events.body: The fishers who leave Caol ìseal's silted harbour carry their nets, their smoking-racks and the small shrine from the harbour's edge, and set the shrine up again at Caol bheag stone by stone in the same order, so that it stands as it always stood.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Caol ìseal fishers go east

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: IV. Of the Fishers Who Went East, and the Lane to the South

events.title: Caol ìseal turns to the plough
events.body: The houses of Caol ìseal nearest the silted water turn to farming the ground behind them after the fishers go east, and within two generations the town that smelled of fish and tar smells, most days, of turned earth.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Caol ìseal fishers go east

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: IV. Of the Fishers Who Went East, and the Lane to the South

events.title: The southern lane
events.body: The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich, on the wild strait of the west coast, take their boats round into the southern sea, along the whole south coast to the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, and up it to the landing of Cidhe Beag below Baile thais, where they sell dried fish for grain. The older harbours of the south coast, which had never sailed beyond their own capes, begin to follow. The lane is named for its first sailors: Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The older southern harbours follow the new lane

events.title: The keel-song of Cuan shean
events.body: Iseabail nic Lachlainn, a gatherer of songs for the royal household, takes down a work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words mean nothing to those who sing it. It is all that survives, in any form, of the craft of the Sundering fleet.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iseabail nic Lachlainn sent out on the king's road

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A rope-maker's guess at the old words

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Òran na Druime read at the king's court

links.label: Same person
links.title: Death of Tormod Ròpaire

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Iseabail's tablets entered in Taigh na Fèithe

events.title: The Stone's schism at Inis thais
events.body: The Stone's congregation at Inis thais divides over whether the dead may be prayed for at Clach. Those who say no keep the temple; the others build a second house at Baile gheal.

events.title: Iseabail nic Lachlainn sent out on the king's road
events.body: The steward of the royal household at Cathair dhearg, wanting a linen-maid's quick-eared daughter out from under his feet, sends her out with a mule and a letter of lodging to gather what the shires' kitchens and rope-walks still sing at their work.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The keel-song of Cuan shean

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: V. Of Iseabail nic Lachlainn

events.title: A rope-maker's guess at the old words
events.body: A young man of Tormod Ròpaire's crew, not yet trusted with the lead, tells the gatherer Iseabail that Òran na Druime's strange words are likely only older speech worn smooth by centuries of mouths that never meant to wear it; Tormod answers that it changes nothing about how the strand is walked.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The keel-song of Cuan shean

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: VI. Of the Rope-Walk at Cuan shean

events.title: Òran na Druime read at the king's court
events.body: Iseabail nic Lachlainn reads her whole gathering before the king's hall at Cathair dhearg, and Òran na Druime's strange lines silence a room grown used to songs it half knows already; an old harper and a clerk of Taigh na Fèithe each say the words fit no tongue or hand they know, and neither can say more than that.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The keel-song of Cuan shean

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: VII. Of the Reading at Court

events.title: The older southern harbours follow the new lane
events.body: A season or two after Caol fhiadhaich's boats are first believed, the older harbours of the south coast, which had never in memory put a boat past their own headlands, begin one after another to follow Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich down to the landing at Cidhe Beag.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The southern lane

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: IV. Of the Fishers Who Went East, and the Lane to the South

events.title: The grey storm at Seann Tarr
events.body: A storm named Gailleann Ghlas comes out of the east and destroys the harbour of Seann Tarr. The village is rebuilt and the harbour is not; its boats go to Cuan ruadh.

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Seann Tarr becomes a village again

events.title: The second wolf-house at Baile gheal
events.body: The dissenters from Inis thais raise their house at Baile gheal and pray there for the dead by name. The two houses of the Stone are not reconciled in this age.

events.title: Death of Tormod Ròpaire
events.body: The rope-maker who led the walk that sang Òran na Druime dies at Cuan shean, seventy years old, having in his last years let a younger man keep the count while he sang on behind him; his crew keeps the song after him exactly as he gave it, no better understood than before.

links.label: Same person
links.title: The keel-song of Cuan shean

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: VI. Of the Rope-Walk at Cuan shean

events.title: Birth of Catrìona Bheag
events.body: A daughter, Catrìona, is born into Clann Raghnaill, the crown's own house; she is small from the cradle, and the house calls her Catrìona Bheag.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: IX. Of the Queen Small and the Grey Glaze

events.title: Seann Tarr becomes a village again
events.body: With its harbour broken past mending and its boats gone to Cuan ruadh, Seann Tarr keeps its houses and its shrine but is entered in the charter-roll, in the roll's own dry word for such places, as a village once more rather than a harbour town.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The grey storm at Seann Tarr

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Schism, the Storm, and the New Harbour

events.title: Cuan ruadh's new harbour
events.body: Cuan ruadh builds a second harbour arm for the boats from Seann Tarr, and thrives on the east-coast fishing for the rest of the age.

events.title: Iseabail's tablets entered in Taigh na Fèithe
events.body: On Iseabail nic Lachlainn's death the household she served the rest of her life sends her whole collection to Taigh na Fèithe, where the clerks write into the inventory that it holds one item they can describe only by its sound and its keeping, not its meaning.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The keel-song of Cuan shean

told_in.book: Of the Keel-Song
told_in.section: X. Of the Song Unexplained

events.title: Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned
events.body: Catrìona Bheag of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg, the first queen in more than three centuries. It is written that she was small, and that no one said so twice.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Birth of Catrìona Bheag

events.title: The grey glaze of Muileann gheal
events.body: The potters of Muileann gheal make a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island can match, and the custodian houses buy it for their tables. The secret is kept within one family, Clann Mhic Phàil.

events.title: The oath of the seven
events.body: Queen Catrìona Bheag has the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth before her, the first renewal of the oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swears last.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Clann Choinnich's head asks the manner of the oath

events.title: Clann Choinnich's head asks the manner of the oath
events.body: Before swearing last to Riaghailt an Teallaich, the head of Clann Choinnich asks Queen Catrìona Bheag plainly whether the renewed oath changes the measure her house holds or only the manner of swearing to it. The queen answers that it changes only the manner, and the old woman swears.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The oath of the seven

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: I. Of the Oath of the Seven

events.title: Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr
events.body: The priests of Macha raise their great house at Cathair mhòr, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr in this age. Its floor of black and white was eleven years in the laying.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The last stone laid in Macha's floor

events.title: The last stone laid in Macha's floor
events.body: The black and white floor of Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr is finished, eleven years in the laying, by masons none of whom cut its first courses. It stands the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: I. Of the Oath of the Seven

events.title: The eastern Toll-dubh
events.body: Charcoal-burners in the east find again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tales, with the same cut stair as the one walled up in the west. The custodians wall this one too, and the scribe binds the two entries of the custody-book each to the other.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Leabhar a' Chùraim binds the two stairs

events.title: Leabhar a' Chùraim binds the two stairs
events.body: When charcoal-burners break into the eastern Toll-dubh, the scribe of Leabhar a' Chùraim binds its entry to the western stair's with a line in each margin, though nothing is written of what either stair goes down to.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The eastern Toll-dubh

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: II. Of the Stair Found Again, and the Dry Years

events.title: The dry years at Achadh shean
events.body: Three dry seasons one after another empty the wells of the eastern shires about Achadh shean. The shared meal holds, and the crown carts grain in from the south.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The well-head board first cut

events.title: The well-head board first cut
events.body: As the crown's grain carts still reach Achadh shean by the mining road against a second dry season, the reeves cut a board at the well-head setting down how the deep wells will be shared among the households by lot and by turn. The board is renewed each generation; the lots themselves are never drawn again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dry years at Achadh shean

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The water-rights of Achadh shean

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: II. Of the Stair Found Again, and the Dry Years

events.title: The water-rights of Achadh shean
events.body: The reeves of Achadh shean share the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn, and write the sharing on a board at the well-head. The board is renewed each generation; the lots are never drawn again.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The well-head board first cut

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The reeve of Achadh shean questioned at the well-head

events.title: A clerk finds the worn firlot
events.body: A young clerk newly set over the granary accounts at Àth shean finds, going back through the ledgers, that the firlot has worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been so for longer than any one reeve's term could account for. He carries the matter up rather than let it stand.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The firlot of Àth shean

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: II. Of the Stair Found Again, and the Dry Years

events.title: The firlot of Àth shean
events.body: The granary of Àth shean finds that its firlot has worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been so for generations. The reeve's accounts are put right as far back as anyone can reckon.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: A clerk finds the worn firlot

events.title: Birth of Sìleas Òg
events.body: A daughter, Sìleas, is born in the house of the crown in the seventy-seventh year of Queen Catrìona Bheag's reign, and called Sìleas Òg after the queen who first measured the island's baskets.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Queen Sìleas Òg crowned

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: V. Of the Silver Refused and the Steel Lost

events.title: Iain Mac Phàil tries to write the glaze down
events.body: In the last years of his life Iain Mac Phàil, the last of Clann Mhic Phàil at Muileann gheal, tries to set the grey-green glaze's making down in some form a stranger might follow, and finds the moment of the kiln's cooling will not go into words.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The grey glaze lost

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: III. Of the Last of Clann Mhic Phàil

events.title: Two apprentices fail the grey-green firing
events.body: Iain Mac Phàil takes two apprentices in his last years and teaches them the mixing of the grey-green glaze, but neither learns to judge the moment the kiln's heat must be let fall. Both come away able to throw a passable dish and unable to glaze it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The grey glaze lost

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: III. Of the Last of Clann Mhic Phàil

events.title: The grey glaze lost
events.body: The last of Clann Mhic Phàil dies at Muileann gheal without passing on the glaze. For a generation the potters of the town try to match it, and fail.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Iain Mac Phàil tries to write the glaze down

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Two apprentices fail the grey-green firing

events.title: Drovers of Àth chiar bring their beasts to Baile Mòr ruadh
events.body: Drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills begin bringing their cattle down to Baile Mòr ruadh's autumn fair rather than selling nearer home, and within a few years it is the greatest fair in the east.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Baile Mòr ruadh's fair

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: III. Of the Last of Clann Mhic Phàil

events.title: Baile Mòr ruadh's fair
events.body: Baile Mòr ruadh in the east holds a cattle fair that draws drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills. It becomes yearly, and the greatest fair in the east.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Drovers of Àth chiar bring their beasts to Baile Mòr ruadh

events.title: Queen Sìleas Òg crowned
events.body: Sìleas Òg of Clann Raghnaill, named for the queen of the firlot, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler known to have visited every shire seat.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Birth of Sìleas Òg

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Sìleas Òg questioned on her purpose

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Sìleas Òg reaches the last shire seat of her round

events.title: Sìleas Òg questioned on her purpose
events.body: Asked years later what put the notion of a round of every shire seat in her head, Queen Sìleas Òg says she had grown up hearing the seats named at her father's table like places in a story, and wished to know them as a place stood in rather than a tale repeated.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Sìleas Òg crowned

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: IV. Of the Queen Who Went Round

events.title: The reeve of Achadh shean questioned at the well-head
events.body: On her round, Sìleas Òg stands at the well-head of Achadh shean and asks the reeve why the lots for the deep wells were never drawn a second time. He answers that no household wished to be the one that named the first sharing unfair. She rides on the next morning without asking him to change it.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The water-rights of Achadh shean

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: IV. Of the Queen Who Went Round

events.title: Sìleas Òg reaches the last shire seat of her round
events.body: Queen Sìleas Òg's circuit carries her at last to the bare northern stretch few rulers before her had visited, the first ruler of Dia-thìr known to have stood in every shire seat the island holds.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Sìleas Òg crowned

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: IV. Of the Queen Who Went Round

events.title: Sìleas Òg's count of hands
events.body: Queen Sìleas Òg commands a new count of every household holding the right to the coal. It is smaller than any before, for the right has narrowed into fewer and larger households, and the queen has it entered without comment.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The queen enters the count without comment

events.title: The queen enters the count without comment
events.body: Reading the new, smaller count of households holding the right to the coal, Sìleas Òg has it entered in Leabhar a' Chùraim without a word either way, a silence her own scribes find harder to read than any word she might have spoken.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Sìleas Òg's count of hands

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: IV. Of the Queen Who Went Round

events.title: The fire of Ceann mhin
events.body: A second great fire burns Ceann mhin, and this time there is no war to blame. By order of its reeve the town is rebuilt with gable walls of stone between the houses.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ceann mhin's reeve orders the gable walls

events.title: Ceann mhin's reeve orders the gable walls
events.body: Before the ash of the second fire has cooled, the reeve of Ceann mhin orders the town rebuilt with gable walls of stone standing between each house and the next, so that a fire must cross stone to spread.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fire of Ceann mhin

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: IV. Of the Queen Who Went Round

events.title: Birth of Ailean the Fourth
events.body: A son, named Ailean mac Raghnaill after the kings of that name before him, is born into the crown's house in the two-and-twentieth year of Queen Sìleas Òg's reign.

links.label: Same person
links.title: King Ailean the Fourth crowned

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: V. Of the Silver Refused and the Steel Lost

events.title: Birth of Mòrag nic Raghnaill
events.body: A daughter, Mòrag, is born to the same house, six years younger than her brother Ailean.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: VI. Of the Short King and the Shut Sea

events.title: Clann Choinnich's clerk drafts Athchuingean an Airgid
events.body: After three winters of the head of Clann Choinnich arguing that the coal might be spared beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, a younger kinsman of the house drafts the petition the council will hear, the first written asking to burn the coal for work rather than worship.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The silver smelt refused

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: V. Of the Silver Refused and the Steel Lost

events.title: The silver smelt refused
events.body: Clann Choinnich asks leave to burn the coal beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, since the coal burns hotter than charcoal. The council refuses. It is the first asking to burn the coal for work and not for worship.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Clann Choinnich's clerk drafts Athchuingean an Airgid

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The queen's word to Clann Choinnich's head

events.title: The queen's word to Clann Choinnich's head
events.body: Once the council's refusal is final, Sìleas Òg tells Clann Choinnich's head privately that a law kept since before the fleet sailed for one reason is not easily bent to a second, however sound. The old woman accepts the courtesy without being persuaded.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The silver smelt refused

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: V. Of the Silver Refused and the Steel Lost

events.title: The last blade of the old folding
events.body: The fellowship of Dùn dhearg loses the last smith trained far enough in the layered steel's folding to finish it alone. The blades made after him are ordinary work, prized now only for what the craft once was.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The lost smithing at Dùn dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: V. Of the Silver Refused and the Steel Lost

events.title: The lost smithing at Dùn dhearg
events.body: The smiths of Dùn dhearg, makers of the ceremonial blades of the custodian houses since the walls were built, lose the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded. After him the blades of Dùn dhearg are ordinary.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The last blade of the old folding

events.title: The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
events.body: The custodian houses begin to bury their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, among graves older than any name on them. The tenants of the land about call it unwise, and go on burying their own dead elsewhere.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The tenants of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach keep their own ground

events.title: The tenants of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach keep their own ground
events.body: When Na Seachd Taighean begin burying their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the tenants of the land about it call the custom unwise and go on burying their own dead where their own families always have, a disagreement neither side presses to settle.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: V. Of the Silver Refused and the Steel Lost

events.title: King Ailean the Fourth crowned
events.body: Ailean mac Raghnaill, fourth king of that name, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered only for the shortest reign in the king-list.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Birth of Ailean the Fourth

links.label: Leads to
links.title: One stone cut for two reigns

events.title: The synod of Manannan's order
events.body: The priests of Manannan meet at Seann Skell and lay down again the rule of sight-of-land. To it they add a prayer, said at the foot of the river pool, that Manannan keep the sea shut: A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The synod argues two days over the prayer's words

events.title: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned
events.body: Ailean's sister Mòrag nic Raghnaill is crowned after him. She reigns forty years, and the king-list has for her its longest run of entries telling of nothing but good harvests and the rite.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Birth of Mòrag nic Raghnaill

links.label: Leads to
links.title: One stone cut for two reigns

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Death of Ailean the Fourth at forty

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A clerk reckons forty quiet years

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The reign of Mòrag nic Raghnaill ends

events.title: One stone cut for two reigns
events.body: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill has the years of her brother Ailean the Fourth's crowning and death cut on a single stone rather than two, the plainest record Clàr nan Rìghrean gives of the short reign she outlives by forty years.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: King Ailean the Fourth crowned

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: VI. Of the Short King and the Shut Sea

events.title: The synod argues two days over the prayer's words
events.body: The priests of Manannan in synod at Seann Skell spend two full days over the wording of a new prayer before agreeing on its shortest form, to be said at the foot of the river pool where the fleet once turned.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The synod of Manannan's order

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: VI. Of the Short King and the Shut Sea

events.title: Death of Ailean the Fourth at forty
events.body: King Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth of the name, dies at Cathair dhearg within the year of his crowning, forty years old; Leabhar a' Chùraim does not say what ailed him, and his sister Mòrag, four-and-thirty, is crowned before the season turns.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: VI. Of the Short King and the Shut Sea

events.title: The ferry at Cidhe Beag
events.body: A ferry family settles at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine and carries folk and goods down the river by canoe. They hold the landing for the rest of the age.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The ferry family holds the landing father to daughter

events.title: The ferry family holds the landing father to daughter
events.body: The family that settles the ferry crossing at Cidhe Beag holds the landing from father to daughter and daughter to son for the rest of the age, a fixed thing on the eastern road like any ford or road-house.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ferry at Cidhe Beag

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: VI. Of the Short King and the Shut Sea

events.title: The dark wine of Àth shean
events.body: The growers on the slopes above Àth shean press blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine that keeps a year in the cask. It is sold along the eastern road, and the road-houses serve it as black wine.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The road-houses take up the black wine

events.title: The road-houses take up the black wine
events.body: The road-houses of the eastern stretch above Àth shean take to serving the growers' dark blaeberry and bramble pressing as black wine, a trade that outlasts a good deal the age's councils thought more likely to last.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dark wine of Àth shean

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: VI. Of the Short King and the Shut Sea

events.title: A clerk reckons forty quiet years
events.body: A clerk who has served Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill the whole of her reign remarks, near the end of his service, that he has written more entries under her than under any three reigns before and set down in all of them no death by war, no famine and no quarrel of Na Seachd Taighean.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned

told_in.book: Of the Queen Who Went Round
told_in.section: VI. Of the Short King and the Shut Sea

events.title: The reign of Mòrag nic Raghnaill ends
events.body: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill's reign ends in her four-and-seventieth year, after forty years crowned; Clàr nan Rìghrean sets down the end of it and little else, as it has set down little else of all her quiet years.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: VII. Of the Roads, the Beasts, and the Empty Harbour Kept Thin

events.title: Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up
events.body: The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr, which had sailed Slighe-uisce fhuar, the cold way along the north coast from Ros chiar to Caol mhin, since the early years of the Sundering, are laid up for good as the roads grow better. The last is kept on the strand as a wonder.

events.title: Earthquake at Dùn ìseal
events.body: An earthquake shakes Dùn ìseal and cracks the spirit-house. No one is killed. The keepers take it for a warning, but cannot agree of what.

events.title: Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies
events.body: Beathag nic Thòmais, widow of a mill-owner of Muileann chaol, begins to buy old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from houses that no longer read them. She keeps them in a loft over her mill.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A cheese-press board sold to the widow of Muileann chaol

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A clerk of Taigh na Fèithe finds a lost ruling in the loft

events.title: A cheese-press board sold to the widow of Muileann chaol
events.body: A carter brings Beathag nic Thòmais a blackened board a Cathair mhòr road house has used for years to weight a cheese-press, having noticed writing on its underside: a coal-right tally three generations old. She pays a fair measure of meal for it, telling the carter that a house's own forgetting is no measure of what a board is worth.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: II. Of the Widow of Muileann chaol

events.title: A clerk of Taigh na Fèithe finds a lost ruling in the loft
events.body: A clerk riding through Muileann chaol on the crown's business climbs the mill stair out of idleness and finds, among Beathag nic Thòmais's boards, the only surviving copy of a custodians' ruling Taigh na Fèithe had lost to fire two generations before. He asks whether she means the loft for the crown's use or her own; she says the question is not hers to answer alone.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: II. Of the Widow of Muileann chaol

events.title: The paper mill at Muileann chaol
events.body: A mill at Muileann chaol begins to make paper from rags, the first on Dia-thìr. In this generation the custody-book is first copied onto paper.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Beathag nic Thòmais presses her own sheet of rag paper

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Beathag carries the proposal of paper to Taigh na Fèithe

events.title: Beathag nic Thòmais presses her own sheet of rag paper
events.body: Having watched Anna nic Coinnich work her pulp-troughs a season, Beathag presses a sheet with her own hands, uneven at one corner, and keeps it apart from the loft's other papers for the rest of her life without ever saying why.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The paper mill at Muileann chaol

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: III. Of the Rag Paper

events.title: Beathag carries the proposal of paper to Taigh na Fèithe
events.body: Beathag nic Thòmais rides the sixty miles to Taigh na Fèithe herself to put Anna's rag paper before a custodian, judging a widow's word better heard than a stranger's. Asked whether the new stuff will hold ink sixteen centuries as hide has, she says she cannot promise it, and the custodian lets the copying go ahead.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The paper mill at Muileann chaol

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: III. Of the Rag Paper

events.title: Three copies of the landfall tidings
events.body: Among her papers Beathag nic Thòmais finds three copies of the tidings of the two landfalls. They differ in the order of the coasts and the number of hulls. She writes out all three side by side and does not choose between them.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Beathag answers Anna on the three copies

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A niece asks why the wrong copies were not burned

events.title: Beathag answers Anna on the three copies
events.body: Found still kneeling over the three tellings of the landfall at dusk, Beathag tells Anna nic Coinnich that she believes all three writers honest and none of their three pasts more true than the others, and that choosing one for comfort's sake would be a falsehood of her own making.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Three copies of the landfall tidings

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: IV. Of the Three Copies

events.title: Birth of Tormod mac Ruairidh
events.body: A son, Tormod, is born to Ruairidh of Clann Raghnaill, the crown's own house, in the years Beathag nic Thòmais is filling her loft at Muileann chaol.

links.label: Same person
links.title: King Tormod mac Ruairidh crowned

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: VII. Of the Roads, the Beasts, and the Empty Harbour Kept Thin

events.title: A niece asks why the wrong copies were not burned
events.body: Hearing the tale of the three copies at the fireside, Beathag's niece asks why the two that disagreed with the truth were not simply burned. Beathag, by then old, tells her this is the very question the loft exists to leave unanswered.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Three copies of the landfall tidings

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: IV. Of the Three Copies

events.title: The north-west coast counted
events.body: The crown sends a reeve to list the households of the thinned north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. He counts fewer households than there are harbour berths.

events.title: The loft at Muileann chaol
events.body: Beathag nic Thòmais dies, and leaves her loft of papers to the town of Muileann chaol on condition that nothing in it be burned. The town keeps that condition and very little else of her wishes.

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The copy of the list sent to the loft at Muileann chaol

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The nephew stumbles reading the loft's condition

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A miller answers a reeve on the town's right to the loft

events.title: The nephew stumbles reading the loft's condition
events.body: Reading Beathag nic Thòmais's will aloud to the assembled kin, her nephew stumbles over the clause forbidding any burning of the loft's papers, and more than one kinsman marks the stumble and thinks the less of him for it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The loft at Muileann chaol

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: VI. Of the Loft Left to the Town

events.title: King Tormod mac Ruairidh crowned
events.body: Tormod mac Ruairidh of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg. His reign is remembered for its roads and its length.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Birth of Tormod mac Ruairidh

events.title: Manannan's harbour prayer
events.body: The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell begin to say their prayer for the shut sea on the day of the rite of the empty harbour, so that both are kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side is pleased.

events.title: Birth of Gormshuil nic Thormoid
events.body: A daughter, Gormshuil, is born at Cathair dhearg to King Tormod mac Ruairidh, five-and-thirty years old and six years crowned.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Death of King Tormod

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: VII. Of the Roads, the Beasts, and the Empty Harbour Kept Thin

events.title: Tormod's bridges
events.body: King Tormod builds stone bridges over the fords of the south-central shires, one of them at Cnoc ìseal. Ferry-keepers who lose their living are given land in amends.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A ferryman chooses the market road over the water

events.title: A ferryman chooses the market road over the water
events.body: Given his choice of two parcels in amends for the bridge that ends his crossing, a ferryman of Cnoc ìseal asks the king's reeve which has the better crossing to the market road, and takes it; his sons never return to the water.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Tormod's bridges

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: VII. Of the Roads, the Beasts, and the Empty Harbour Kept Thin

events.title: The panther year
events.body: The panthers cross the southern roads in numbers beyond any herder's memory, and for a whole season the crossing days run into one another. Flocks are kept in folds from Cnoc àrsaidh to the coast.

events.title: A miller answers a reeve on the town's right to the loft
events.body: A crown reeve asks Beathag nic Thòmais's great-nephew, by then the loft's unpaid keeper, what right the town has to papers that belong by their matter to Taigh na Fèithe or the crown. He answers that fifty years of neither office asking for them back is itself an answer.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The loft at Muileann chaol

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: VI. Of the Loft Left to the Town

events.title: Caol gharbh loses the salt
events.body: The sea rises over the salt pans of Caol gharbh and they fail, and salt comes to the north-east from the south instead. The town that took the trade of Ros fhionn is poorer than Ros fhionn had been.

events.title: Storm at Baile ghorm
events.body: A south-westerly storm floods the low town of Baile ghorm and drowns twenty-three. The town raises its sea-wall by the height of a man.

events.title: A scribe questions the last keepers of the rite
events.body: Sent to note Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh for the crown's book, a scribe asks the last old women of Seann Skell on what day the fleet truly sailed. No two answers agree, and he writes as much into the crown's own book, unable to choose among them any more than Beathag nic Thòmais once could among her three copies.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The rite kept by few

told_in.book: Of the Loft over the Mill
told_in.section: VII. Of the Roads, the Beasts, and the Empty Harbour Kept Thin

events.title: The rite kept by few
events.body: The rite of the empty harbour on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell is kept by the harbour priests and a few old families. A visiting scribe writes that none there could say on what day the fleet had in truth sailed.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: A scribe questions the last keepers of the rite

events.title: Cuan dhearg flooded again
events.body: The sea comes over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg a second time, and the street moved back after An Gàire Dubh is flooded to the thresholds. The town builds a sea-wall and does not move again.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil carries the harbour-master's counsel to the king

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Cuan dhearg buries its own boundary stones

events.title: Gormshuil carries the harbour-master's counsel to the king
events.body: Sent by her father to see the sea-wall building at Cuan dhearg, Gormshuil nic Thormoid hears the harbour-master say a wall a man can stand behind is worth more than a street he can only run from, and rides home to give the king the counsel word for word.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cuan dhearg flooded again

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: I. Of the Sea-Wall of Cuan dhearg

events.title: Cuan dhearg buries its own boundary stones
events.body: Rather than break up the boundary stones of the street the sea first moved, Cuan dhearg buries them on the chance a later hand may want to know how far the water once came.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cuan dhearg flooded again

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: I. Of the Sea-Wall of Cuan dhearg

events.title: The house at Dùn thais reopened
events.body: The house of disputation at Dùn thais, shut and opened more than once since the table of years, is opened again on condition that the question of longer lives is not raised. The druids of the schools accept it and argue about the vein instead.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The schools take up the question of the vein instead

events.title: The schools take up the question of the vein instead
events.body: Reopened on condition that the question of longer lives is never raised again, Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais turns instead to whether Leabhar a' Chùraim's measure of the handful answers rightly to what the coal gives out.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The house at Dùn thais reopened

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: II. Of the House Reopened at Dùn thais

events.title: Death of King Tormod
events.body: King Tormod mac Ruairidh dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. His daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Birth of Gormshuil nic Thormoid

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The king's last night

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil crowned at one-and-fifty

events.title: The king's last night
events.body: Tormod mac Ruairidh tells his daughter Gormshuil, on the last night of his seven-and-fifty-year reign, that he never once found courage to ask Taigh na Fèithe a question Taigh na Deasbaid was forbidden to ask on his behalf, and that finding it will be the easier half of her trouble.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Death of King Tormod

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: III. Of the Death of the King

events.title: Gormshuil crowned at one-and-fifty
events.body: Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned in An Talla Dearg a fortnight after her father's death, the same age he had been when the sea-wall of Cuan dhearg was still only a plan on a tally-stick.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Death of King Tormod

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: I. Of the Sea-Wall of Cuan dhearg

events.title: Queen Gormshuil's progress
events.body: Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid rides round every shire seat of the island, the first ruler to do so since Sìleas Òg. Her clerks write down the grievances of each shire; the queen answers none of them in writing.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A boundary measured and not judged

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Leabhar nan Gearan opened at every seat

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A reeve asks the queen what the writing is for

events.title: A boundary measured and not judged
events.body: At the first seat of her progress a householder accuses her neighbour of shifting a boundary stone by moonlight three years running; Gormshuil measures the disputed ground herself and has it written down, so that the writing, not the queen, will settle it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Gormshuil's progress

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: IV. Of the Progress and the Book of Grievances

events.title: Leabhar nan Gearan opened at every seat
events.body: At every shire seat of Queen Gormshuil's progress, in the sixth year of her reign and her seven-and-fiftieth of life, her clerks open Leabhar nan Gearan and write down each seat's grievance in the shire's own words.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Gormshuil's progress

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: IV. Of the Progress and the Book of Grievances

events.title: A reeve asks the queen what the writing is for
events.body: A plain-spoken reeve asks Gormshuil why she writes down every shire's grievance and answers none of them; she tells him a hasty answer given before hearing the whole round is a false ease, and rides on.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Queen Gormshuil's progress

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: IV. Of the Progress and the Book of Grievances

events.title: The second silver petition
events.body: Clann Choinnich asks again to burn the coal beyond the measure for the silver smelt at Muileann chiar, now with three of the seven houses behind it. Queen Gormshuil's council refuses by one voice. The name of the member who changed his vote is written down; his reason is not.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Aonghas mac Lachlainn turns his vote

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil asks Aonghas his reason and is refused

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Death of Aonghas mac Lachlainn

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: A rider of Muileann chiar attends the burying he was never asked to

events.title: Aonghas mac Lachlainn turns his vote
events.body: Meaning by every account to vote with the three houses behind Athchuingean an Airgid, Aonghas mac Lachlainn changes his vote at the board itself and gives no reason beyond the bare word that he has changed his mind.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The second silver petition

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: V. Of the Silver Petition Refused

events.title: Gormshuil asks Aonghas his reason and is refused
events.body: Gormshuil asks Aonghas mac Lachlainn privately why he turned his vote; he answers that a man's reason for his own hand at the board is his to keep, and she lets the matter lie as Leabhar a' Chùraim lets it lie.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The second silver petition

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: V. Of the Silver Petition Refused

events.title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach
events.body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the eastern road feeds the queen's progress with pan-fried spinach and black wine, as the charter-roll records. Its keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, is spared her road dues for a year.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Peigi feeds the queen's whole progress unwarned

events.title: Peigi feeds the queen's whole progress unwarned
events.body: Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, keeper of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, feeds Gormshuil's whole company on pan-fried spinach and black wine though her charter allows stores for far less; the queen forgives her a year's road dues.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: IV. Of the Progress and the Book of Grievances

events.title: The last count of hands
events.body: The vein-house counts for the last time in this age the households holding the right to the coal. They are fewer than at any count before, and greater; the custody-book notes that three of the seven houses now hold more than half the right between them.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A smaller house is granted its neighbour's unused right

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Three houses hold more than half the right

events.title: A smaller house is granted its neighbour's unused right
events.body: At the last Cunntas nan Làmh the custodians grant a house whose share has fallen too low to keep its hearth measure a neighbour's unused coal-right, though more than one voice warns that a house asking twice can be eased once but not mended for good.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The last count of hands

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: VI. Of the Last Count of Hands

events.title: Three houses hold more than half the right
events.body: Leabhar a' Chùraim's clerk notes under the last Cunntas nan Làmh, in the dry hand kept since Donnchadh's day, that three of Na Seachd Taighean now hold more than half the whole right to the coal among themselves.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The last count of hands

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: VI. Of the Last Count of Hands

events.title: Timber out of the mist
events.body: A worked timber, longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith of Dia-thìr knows, comes ashore at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast, from beyond Manannan's mist, as the fishers say. It is carried to Seann Skell, shown to Manannan's priests, and burned.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fishers of Ceann mhòr find the timber

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The oldest crowned ruler since Clàr nam Bliadhnachan

events.title: The fishers of Ceann mhòr find the timber
events.body: Fishers working the empty water off Ceann mhòr, where Faire a' Chinn has long lapsed, find a worked timber cast up, longer than any island tree and fastened with nails no smith on Dia-thìr forged; the eldest among them says hands that made such nails did not make them on the island.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Timber out of the mist

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: VII. Of the Timber Out of the Mist

events.title: The queen goes up to Taigh na Fèithe for the winter burning
events.body: Eighty years old, Gormshuil nic Thormoid rides the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe for the winter burning as she has every year of her reign, and walks her own horse up the last, iced mile rather than let another hand lead it.

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Winter Burning She Did Not Come Down From

events.title: The oldest crowned ruler since Clàr nam Bliadhnachan
events.body: Riding up to the winter burning at eighty, Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid is the oldest ruler Leabhar a' Chùraim has entered crowned and still reigning since long before Clàr nam Bliadhnachan, nine-and-twenty years crowned.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Timber out of the mist

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Winter Burning She Did Not Come Down From

events.title: The council sits in the queen's empty place
events.body: With no word of Gormshuil since the winter burning, the custodians of Na Seachd Taighean meet at An Talla Dearg in the place the crown's own chair has always stood empty for her progress, and send their word up the coal-road by the same riders who carried the crown's business all her reign.

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Winter Burning She Did Not Come Down From

events.title: A crown letter sealed with no name above the seal
events.body: The custodians seal their letters with Taigh na Fèithe's trellis and hollow stone as every crown letter has been sealed since Dòmhnall Ruadh joined the two, but set no name above the seal, and no clerk is ever asked to explain the blank space.

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Winter Burning She Did Not Come Down From

events.title: The lamps at Seann Skell go out
events.body: Fewer houses at Seann Skell keep the night of lamps each year, and at last none on the waterfront. An old woman sets a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe writes that it was she and not the town.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ealasaid nic Iain keeps the last lamp

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ealasaid nic Iain's lamp goes dark

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Eòghann mac Nèill keeps the book with the window dark

events.title: Ealasaid nic Iain keeps the last lamp
events.body: With no household left on the Seann Skell waterfront still keeping Oidhche nan Lòchran, an old woman, Ealasaid nic Iain, sets the one lamp that burns in the harbour-house window; the scribe writes that the lamp was hers and not the town's.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The lamps at Seann Skell go out

told_in.book: Of the Queen's Progress
told_in.section: IX. Of the Last Lamp at Seann Skell

events.title: Ealasaid nic Iain's lamp goes dark
events.body: Ealasaid nic Iain, who alone had kept a lamp burning in the harbour-house window at Seann Skell after the rest of the waterfront let the custom lapse, dies in her own bed, and no one after her sets a light there again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The lamps at Seann Skell go out

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: I. Of the Eleven at Cidhe an Diosail

events.title: The last rite of the empty harbour in this age
events.body: Eleven people keep the rite of the empty harbour at Seann Skell. The harbour scribe enters their number, the weather and the state of the tide, and nothing more.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eòghann mac Nèill counts the rite of the eleven

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eòghann mac Nèill keeps the book with the window dark

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The last winter of the age

events.title: Eòghann mac Nèill counts the rite of the eleven
events.body: At Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh on Cidhe an Diosail, Eòghann mac Nèill, eleven years the quay's scribe, stands back as the scribe's place requires and counts the people on the stones twice, once by eye and once by name: eleven.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The last rite of the empty harbour in this age

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: I. Of the Eleven at Cidhe an Diosail

events.title: Death of Aonghas mac Lachlainn
events.body: Aonghas mac Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg, four-and-eighty years old, the last of the council that had refused Clann Choinnich's Athchuingean an Airgid; asked once more on his deathbed why he had turned his own vote, he answers only that his reason had not stopped seeming good to him, and says no more.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The second silver petition

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The silver petition laid aside

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: II. Of the Petition Laid Aside

events.title: A rider of Muileann chiar attends the burying he was never asked to
events.body: A rider sent down by the silver guild of Muileann chiar on the strength of an old courtesy stands at the back of Aonghas mac Lachlainn's small burying at Cathair dhearg, and no one there asks him why a guild his vote had cost a fortune troubled to send anyone at all.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The second silver petition

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: II. Of the Petition Laid Aside

events.title: The silver petition laid aside
events.body: The member who had turned the vote being dead, Clann Choinnich does not bring its silver petition to the council again. It lies unanswered in the vein-house, and the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Death of Aonghas mac Lachlainn

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Na Seachd Taighean name themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Clann Choinnich's question is set aside at the first sitting

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The queen's chair is left standing empty

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The council's letters keep no name above the seal

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Talla Dearg holds five hundred souls

events.title: Eòghann mac Nèill keeps the book with the window dark
events.body: Eòghann mac Nèill, harbour scribe of Seann Skell, passes the harbour-house window each rite-day and finds no reason offered for a light to be set there again; he enters nothing of it in his own book, which is kept for the number, the weather and the tide alone.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The lamps at Seann Skell go out

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The last rite of the empty harbour in this age

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: I. Of the Eleven at Cidhe an Diosail

events.title: Na Seachd Taighean name themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim
events.body: Meeting at Cathair dhearg by chance of their riders' errands rather than by any summons, the heads of Na Seachd Taighean call themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim, the council of the custody, and name Tormod mac Ailein, eight-and-thirty years old and a custodian's son of no house among the seven, Ceann a' Chùraim to speak for them with one voice.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The silver petition laid aside

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: III. Of the Chair Left Empty

events.title: Clann Choinnich's question is set aside at the first sitting
events.body: At the same sitting that names the council of the custody, Clann Choinnich alone asks whether the silver might be raised again; the board sets the question aside mildly, unwilling to test a new council on the one asking that had already cost the last one a member's death.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The silver petition laid aside

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: III. Of the Chair Left Empty

events.title: The queen's chair is left standing empty
events.body: Na Seachd Taighean leave the chair at the head of the board, the queen's own, standing empty at every sitting after her name is no longer spoken; Tormod mac Ailein, offered it, keeps his place at the board's foot instead, and in time no clerk living can say with certainty whose absence the chair still marks.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The silver petition laid aside

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: III. Of the Chair Left Empty

events.title: The council's letters keep no name above the seal
events.body: The newly named council of the custody sends out its letters from Cathair dhearg sealed with Taigh na Fèithe's own trellis and hollow stone and no name written above the seal, continuing without comment a custom An Talla Dearg's clerks had already begun in the queen's last silent years.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The silver petition laid aside

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: III. Of the Chair Left Empty

events.title: An Talla Dearg holds five hundred souls
events.body: In the year Na Seachd Taighean name their council, An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg holds perhaps five hundred souls in all its lanes and closes, fewer than the tenants of a single one of Na Seachd Taighean in a good year.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The silver petition laid aside

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: III. Of the Chair Left Empty

events.title: The mist thins
events.body: The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell write that the mist on the eastern sea, which has hidden Dia-thìr from every ship beyond it since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it, lies thinner each winter. They say their prayer, A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte, at every tide, and on still mornings the fishers of the north-west coast begin to see the line of the open sea beyond the headlands.

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Manannan's priests keep the tide-prayer through the forty days

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mànas mac Dhùghaill writes that the mist lies thinner

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Oighrig nic Eachainn sees the line of the open sea

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Oighrig keeps what she saw to her own mother

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The last winter of the age

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eòghann mac Nèill at the last winter

events.title: Mànas mac Dhùghaill writes that the mist lies thinner
events.body: Mànas mac Dhùghaill, priest of Manannan's rite at Seann Skell, sets down for the first time in his own book a thing the older priests had only ever said at the hearth: that the grey past the headlands stands thinner each year, and that he cannot say whether saying the prayer at every tide holds anything back at all.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mist thins

told_in.book: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist
told_in.section: IV. Of the Fisher of Ceann mhòr

events.title: Oighrig nic Eachainn sees the line of the open sea
events.body: A fisher of Ceann mhòr, Oighrig nic Eachainn, rests on her oars past where the rule of sight-of-land strictly allows and sees, for a few breaths before the grey closes again, a hard dark line beyond the mist, ruled clean across the edge of the world.

events.title: Oighrig keeps what she saw to her own mother
events.body: Oighrig nic Eachainn turns for home as the rule says and tells no priest and no reeve what she saw beyond the mist, speaking of it months after only to her own mother, who tells her she has already shown better sense in the keeping of it than most who see such things at all.

events.title: The last winter of the age
events.body: On a still morning near the year's dark heart, the priests of Manannan pray at every tide at Seann Skell, the boats of Ceann mhòr turn for home before the rule strictly asks it of them, and the council keeps its board at Cathair dhearg with the chair at its head still empty, while the harbour-house lamp-window that once marked Oidhche nan Lòchran stands dark for another winter.

events.title: Eòghann mac Nèill at the last winter
events.body: Six-and-twenty years the scribe of Cidhe an Diosail, Eòghann mac Nèill walks down to the stones each Là an Diosail with the same board under his arm and writes the number, the weather and the tide in the same plain hand.
